4432622e6ac07df5: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 15 — All major operational systems, as well as the Ministry of Health’s (MOH) healthcare and patient treatment services, remain unaffected and are operating as usual following a cybersecurity incident detected on Thursday (Nov 12).
MOH said in a statement posted on Facebook yesterday that the public can continue with healthcare appointments and treatment at its facilities without cause for concern.
The ministry said the incident was limited to unauthorised access to a support file storage and sharing platform at one of its facilities.
“An initial investigation by MOH’s Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) found that the incident did not involve the encryption of the ministry’s main databases,” the statement said.

The ministry said it immediately blocked public access to the platform to contain the incident and introduced additional security measures at the affected facility, including user password resets, server audits, and mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Under the Cyber Security Act 2024 (Act 854), the ministry will continue working closely with the National Cyber Security Agency (Nacsa) to address the incident and monitor continuously to safeguard cybersecurity.
Meanwhile, MOH advised the public to remain calm and refrain from speculation.
“MOH strongly warns that downloading, possessing or distributing official government documents obtained unlawfully constitutes a serious offence and is subject to legal action,” it said.

The ministry also reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining the highest level of security for its information technology infrastructure and protecting the confidentiality of the public’s health data. — Bernama
9a4758eb013a28aa: STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.
50a631e8bdabf00e: INDIAN WELLS, (California): Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva extended her unbeaten run at the WTA Finals on Saturday, dispatching American Jessica Pegula 6-3 6-4 to reach the final, where she will face a resurgent Elina Svitolina.
Andreeva's heavy groundstrokes, strong serving and tireless defense were too much for the American in their first career meeting, played under sunny skies in the California desert.
"It was a tough match," Andreeva said.
"You have to work hard to win a point against her. She is going to leave everything out there and make your life complicated, so I wanted to make her life complicated as well today."
The opening set was tight until Andreeva pounced on a looping shot from Pegula and drilled a forehand winner to break serve for a 5-3 lead.

Pegula, backed by a supportive crowd, earned break points as Andreeva served for the set, but shanked an overhead and Andreeva took the set two points later when her opponent's backhand found the net.
Pegula broke to grab a 3-1 advantage in the second set but the lead would prove short-lived.
Andreeva broke straight back with a deft volley and broke again to lead 4-3.
The tournament's third seed ultimately sealed the win when a Pegula backhand sailed long on match point.
Andreeva, making her WTA Finals debut, has not dropped a set in four matches at the event.
Svitolina shines
She will face sixth seed Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final after the Ukrainian needed just over an hour to cruise past Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova 6-2 6-1 in Saturday's other semi-final.
Despite strong sun shining in her eyes, Svitolina delivered a crosscourt backhand winner to claim the first set.
She raced out to a 5-0 lead in the second and raised her arms in triumph and beamed a smile after Noskova's forehand went wide on match point.
Andreeva holds a 2-1 lead in their head-to-head matchups, including a one-sided 6-4 6-0 victory in their round-robin match on Monday, but Svitolina has raised her level since.
"It's going to be another big challenge, of course, and I feel I have to do my homework," she said.
"But I feel I'm a completely different player from the first match. I was not playing the right way. I will give it my best shot."
Svitolina has now made the final all three times she has competed in the eight-player championships, winning it in 2018.

c27ed960480c6d20: PETALING JAYA: To humans, a patch of cat urine is generally something to clean up as quickly as possible. To another cat, however, it may contain considerably more useful information.

Scientists have identified a group of unusual chemicals in domestic cat urine that appear to form a distinctive signature for each animal - effectively a chemical calling card that remains relatively stable after the scent is deposited.
The international study, led by researchers at Japan's Iwate University and published in "Current Biology", identified 13 branched-chain fatty acids (BFAs) in cat urine.
What mattered was not simply whether those compounds were present, but their proportions: each cat produced its own characteristic combination.
The researchers also found that the profile remained comparatively consistent when the same animals were sampled at different times.
Related cats tended to have more similar profiles, suggesting genetics may play some role, although individual animals could still be distinguished from one another.

Cats rely heavily on scent to gather information about their surroundings and other animals. Urine marking allows that information to remain in the environment even after the animal responsible has moved on.
The puzzle for scientists was how such a scent could continue conveying identity when many of the chemicals responsible for smell evaporate or change over time.
BFAs may provide part of the answer: unlike highly volatile compounds that disappear relatively quickly, the newly identified fatty acids evaporate more slowly.
In laboratory tests, individual BFA patterns remained comparatively stable for at least 24 hours after urine was deposited.

The cats themselves also appeared able to tell those chemical profiles apart. When researchers repeatedly presented the same urine scent, the animals gradually lost interest, but began investigating again when urine from a different cat was introduced.
They could also distinguish samples in which researchers altered the BFA component while keeping other urinary lipids the same.
The clue inside a cat's kidneys

The research produced another intriguing finding. Scientists traced the BFAs to lipid droplets stored in the renal cortex - structures in cat kidneys that have been known to researchers for more than a century, but whose purpose has remained unclear.
The team suggests these droplets may act as a reservoir, helping stabilise the mix of fatty acids entering the urine despite short-term changes in diet or physiology.

Similar chemical and kidney characteristics were also identified across other members of the cat family, although the experts caution that it has not yet been established whether wild felids use the same system to recognise individuals.

For now, the study offers a striking glimpse into a sensory world humans largely miss. What smells like an unpleasant household accident to us may, to another cat, contain something closer to a nametag or calling card.
44e9b3c17473cdef: PETALING JAYA: Kerjasama Perikatan Nasional (PN) dengan Barisan Nasional (BN) pada PRN Melaka masih belum mampu mengatasi defisit kepercayaan pengundi bukan Melayu terhadap PAS, sekali gus menyukarkan usaha menembusi kubu kuat DAP, menurut penganalisis.

Syaza Shukri dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia (UIAM) berkata walaupun kedua-dua gabungan bekerjasama untuk menarik sokongan merentas kaum, mereka masih gagal meyakinkan pengundi di kawasan yang dikuasai DAP.
"BN yang dilihat lebih inklusif daripada PN pun sukar menembusi kerusi DAP, apatah lagi PN dipimpin PAS.
"Saya percaya kerjasama ini masih tidak cukup dan 'trust deficit' bukan Melayu terhadap PAS masih tinggi," katanya kepada FMT.

Pada PRN Melaka, PN memenangi tiga daripada lima kerusi ditandinginya, termasuk dua menerusi PAS di Bukit Katil dan Paya Rumput, manakala penyandang Bemban, Dr Yadzil Yaakub daripada Wawasan, berjaya mempertahankan kerusinya.
DAP pula mengekalkan semua empat kerusi ditandinginya iaitu Ayer Keroh, Kesidang, Kota Laksamana dan Bandar Hilir.
Parti itu menewaskan komponen PN iaitu Wawasan dan Gerakan di Ayer Keroh serta Kesidang manakala MCA di Kota Laksamana dan Bandar Hilir.
Awang Azman Awang Pawi dari Universiti Malaya berkata penyatuan undi Melayu menerusi kerjasama BN-PN tidak semestinya diterjemahkan kepada penerimaan dalam kalangan pengundi pelbagai kaum.
Beliau berkata walaupun PN mengetengahkan calon daripada Gerakan dan parti komponen lain, gabungan itu masih dikaitkan dengan identiti politik PAS, terutama dalam kalangan pengundi bandar.
"Pemindahan undi antara BN dengan PN tidak berlaku secara seragam mengikut komposisi etnik.

"Kekuatan Umno dan PAS menggembleng sokongan Melayu tidak semestinya mampu mengubah kecenderungan pengundi bukan Melayu yang lama menyokong DAP," katanya merujuk keputusan di Ayer Keroh, apabila calon Gerakan gagal menewaskan DAP di kawasan campuran itu.
"Ia gambaran cabaran PN untuk menarik sokongan lebih luas daripada pengundi bukan Melayu," katanya.
81b93746b294da54: PETALING JAYA: The results of the Melaka polls underscores PAS’s failure to win over non-Malay voters despite its alliance with Barisan Nasional, according to an analyst.

This trust deficit the Islamic party has among non-Malay voters, Syaza Shukri said, will make it difficult for Perikatan Nasional - of which PAS is the lynchpin - to make inroads into DAP strongholds.
“If BN, which is seen to be more inclusive compared with PN, has trouble making inroads in DAP seats, what more a PAS-led PN.
“This trust deficit among non-Malays remains high. The alliance (between PN and BN) isn’t enough (to reduce it),” Syaza, of International Islamic University Malaysia, told FMT.
DAP retained four seats yesterday, namely Ayer Keroh, Kesidang, Kota Laksamana and Bandar Hilir.
The party defeated PN components Wawasan and Gerakan in Ayer Keroh and Kesidang, respectively, while BN component, MCA lost to DAP in Kota Laksamana and Bandar Hilir.
Awang Azman Pawi of Universiti Malaya said while BN and PN managed to consolidate the Malay votes, the alliance struggled to appeal to the non-Malay electorate.
He said despite the likes of Gerakan and other non-Malay components in PN, urban voters still found it difficult to divorce it from PAS’s identity politics.
“Umno and PAS may have succeeded in winning the Malay votes but they did little to sway non-Malay voters who were more inclined to back DAP.
“And this (election) is a glimpse of PN’s challenge to come, wooing the non-Malay voters.”
91cf0d705e0825b1: MILAN: Italian regulators fined Facebook parent company Meta 805 million euros (US$880 million) for accessing users' photos without their "specific" consent, the country's data protection authority said on Saturday.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them", the authority said in a statement.
Meta said it would appeal the decision.
A company spokesperson said "we strongly disagree" with the assessment by the regulators "and the disproportionate level of the fine."

In late October, authorities in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion for having misled the state's residents for more than a decade over use of their data – a record fine for the company, which slammed it as a "tax" on freedom of expression.
Saturday's latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
In 2021, Amazon received a more than 1.1-billion-euro fine for breaching competition law.
That sum was subsequently reduced to 752 million euros on appeal.

The Italian penalty imposed on Facebook relates to its gallery suggestions feature, available since 2023, which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts as they are browsing.

According to Italy's regulator, Facebook requested access to the gallery via a single authorisation valid for the entire app, preceded by a generic notice requesting enabling of other features, which did not allow users to understand that they were also authorising suggestions from their gallery.

The regulator said Meta would now have to seek consent by means of a separate and specific request for the feature concerned and clearly signpost what it is used for, namely that it involves access to a user's photo gallery, as well as how to disable it.

In determining the size of the fine, the authority said it took into account "the high number of people affected" – around 20 million Android users in Italy – and the duration of the infringement, "which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system."
The authority also cited "Meta's lack of cooperation during the investigation."
It imposed a fine amounting to roughly 0.4 per cent of the group's annual turnover, which hit US$201 billion in 2025, for a net profit of US$60.5 billion.--AFP
80c8fcc6985c6717: PARIS: Tens of thousands of protesters paraded in the streets of France on Saturday, some clambering up statues with French flags as they vented on issues ranging from the rising cost of living to a proposal to give police greater legal protection.

The European Union's second-largest economy has been gripped by high-school blockades and mass demonstrations for more than a month, with the far right leading in the polls to win presidential elections next year to replace Emmanuel Macron.
Around 106,000 people took to the streets nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said, in the lowest turnout in recent weeks.
Student unions put the number of demonstrators at 200,000, including almost 100,000 in the capital.

Arrest figures were also noticeably lower than at previous mass protests, with the ministry saying 219 people had been detained across the nation. Paris prosecutors said 45 were arrested in the capital.
"No justice, no peace," a protester shouted into a megaphone in Paris as people including students, unions and Yellow Vest activists demonstrated for the fifth Saturday in a row.
Others called for the president to resign, or cried "Everybody hates the police", as a group carried a giant puppet whose hat read "Lord Macron".
Some of the largely peaceful rallies in recent weeks have seen fringe violence, as well as accusations of police brutality, including against young teenagers.
Giving us hope
Adrien, a 20-year-old cello player in a volunteer orchestra at the Paris rally, said the focus of the day was a new bill in parliament to give police who use their weapons further protection.
"We're scared when we come to a protest, and this will only make us even more afraid if their impunity is strengthened," he said, after tear gas fell on protesting musicians last month.

Backers of the new police bill -- including the far-right party of leading presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen -- say a new law presuming police acted in self-defence is necessary to avoid officers being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force.

Activists argue it would amount to a "licence to kill", as it would hamper the opening of investigations and make holding security forces accountable even harder in a country where alleged police brutality cases rarely reach a criminal court.
Others nationwide demanded better learning conditions, more children's rights or simply sang for a better France.
In the southwestern city of Bordeaux, 72-year-old Josette belted out the protest song "I have two passions: brass bands and revolution".
"My children didn't want me to come," she told AFP. "But I'm so grateful to the youth for starting this movement."
"They're giving us hope at a time when it feels like we're heading straight for disaster, with a planet that keeps getting hotter and far-right movements that are increasingly unapologetic."
Repression unacceptable

Macron's popularity is the lowest it has ever been since he first became president in 2017, according to recent polls, and the government has little leeway to respond to protester demands as it struggles to reduce its debt.
Polls project hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon as runner-up in next year's elections, with the centre-right struggling to present a single strong contender.
In the southern city of Toulouse, Kenza, a 28-year-old asylum law specialist, denounced the government's response to the social unrest.
"The repression of protesters is unacceptable -- even more so when they are children," she said.
Lawyers last week said police violence at recent protests had led to "mutilations" including hand, foot and eye injuries.
Saturday's rallies were largely peaceful but police fired teargas in Paris, Bordeaux and the western city of Nantes, including after some individuals shot fireworks.
Police had to intervene in the city of Lyon to protect a team of television reporters after protesters attacked them, local authorities said.
Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday, after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as "crumbs".
The largest protests in recent weeks occurred during a union-led strike on Thursday last week, when more than half a million people took to the streets nationwide, according to official figures.

bcb260e3103cbbdb: PETALING JAYA: AirBorneo may now be owned by Sarawak, but federal subsidies for rural air services remain crucial to ensure residents continue to have access to affordable air travel, especially in areas with limited alternative transport options.
Economist Firdausi Suffian said the need for subsidies should be assessed based on their importance to residents, rather than solely on who owns the airline.
“Without subsidies, transport costs could be much higher, so these subsidies are necessary to help people maintain access, especially in rural areas,” he told FMT.
Under Budget 2027, the federal government is continuing its RM209 million subsidy for rural flights to remote communities in Sabah and Sarawak, benefitting about 820,000 passengers.
The subsidy was maintained despite the transfer of MASwings to Sarawak and its rebranding as AirBorneo, which took effect on Jan 1 this year.

The subsidy funds rural air services (RAS) under a public service obligation (PSO) to ensure essential routes to interior communities continue operating, even where they may not be commercially viable.
However, not all AirBorneo routes receive subsidies.
The transport ministry previously clarified that the Kuching-Sibu, Kuching-Miri and Kuching-Bintulu routes do not fall under RAS and can be operated commercially.
Flights save time, vital during emergencies
For primary school teacher Gwynth Vincent, 33, flights between Kota Kinabalu and Lahad Datu have saved considerable time, particularly during family emergencies or when seeking medical treatment.
Gwynth, who works in Kota Kinabalu, said travelling by road to her hometown in Lahad Datu would take about eight hours, compared with just 50 minutes by air.
She had previously relied on flights to return home when her grandmother fell ill, and to seek specialist eye treatment in Kota Kinabalu.
“During emergencies, time is very important,” she said.
She said travelling by road was not only time-consuming and exhausting, but could also be risky, particularly when driving at night along poorly maintained and unlit roads.

Another civil servant, Michael Roman, 28, also prefers flying for work-related trips between Kota Kinabalu and the various districts along Sabah's east coast, including Lahad Datu, Sandakan and Tawau.
He said flights took about 45 minutes to an hour, compared with eight to 10 hours by road.
Michael recalled taking the last flight from Lahad Datu to Kota Kinabalu when his uncle was critically ill in hospital.
He said the cost of flying was not significantly different from travelling by road once fuel, meals and, in some cases, rest stops or overnight accommodation were taken into account.
He welcomed government assistance to keep flights accessible, but hoped both the federal and state governments would accelerate road improvements to give residents more transport options.
In Sarawak, civil servant Nuruddin Sabali, 32, uses AirBorneo for work, including trips between Kuching and Mukah, as well as Miri, Limbang and Lawas.

He said RAS subsidies should be maintained because rural flights not only made it easier for residents to travel to major towns, but were also essential for transporting supplies and accessing healthcare.
“Removing the subsidies would increase costs for rural residents,” he said.
Nuruddin said infrastructure conditions in Sabah and Sarawak also differed from those in the peninsula, making air travel essential for some communities.
Access, not just profits
Firdausi said the value of rural flights should not be measured solely by profitability, as the services provided essential access to communities with limited road connections.

He said that besides helping residents obtain medical treatment, flights also facilitated the transport of medical supplies and enabled students from remote areas to pursue their education in towns and cities.
The need for subsidies could diminish if road networks and land transport options improved, said Firdausi.
However, he said the government must ensure that these essential services remain available.
“When residents face difficulties accessing essential services, the government has a role to play through subsidies.
“This is not about whether the investment is productive, but about the welfare of the people,” he said.
bc103e92aa482a30: PETALING JAYA: AirBorneo kini dimiliki Sarawak, namun subsidi kerajaan persekutuan bagi penerbangan pedalaman masih diperlukan bagi memastikan penduduk terus mempunyai akses kepada pengangkutan udara mampu milik, terutama di kawasan dengan pilihan perjalanan terhad.
Ahli ekonomi Firdausi Suffian berkata keperluan subsidi itu harus dinilai berdasarkan kepentingannya kepada penduduk, bukannya semata-mata siapa yang memiliki syarikat penerbangan berkenaan.
“Tanpa subsidi, kos pengangkutan boleh menjadi jauh lebih tinggi, jadi subsidi ini diperlukan untuk membantu penduduk mendapatkan akses, terutama di luar bandar,” katanya kepada FMT.

Menerusi Belanjawan 2027, kerajaan persekutuan meneruskan subsidi RM209 juta bagi penerbangan pedalaman yang dijangka memanfaatkan kira-kira 820,000 penumpang, selepas MASwings diserahkan kepada Sarawak dan dijenamakan semula sebagai AirBorneo.

Subsidi itu membiayai perkhidmatan udara luar bandar (RAS) di bawah obligasi perkhidmatan awam bagi memastikan laluan penting ke kawasan pedalaman terus dikendalikan walaupun mungkin tidak berdaya maju secara komersial.

Bagaimanapun, bukan semua laluan AirBorneo menerima subsidi. Kementerian Pengangkutan sebelum ini menjelaskan laluan Kuching-Sibu, Kuching-Miri dan Kuching-Bintulu bukan dalam kategori RAS dan boleh dikendalikan secara komersial.
Penerbangan jimat masa, penting ketika kecemasan
Bagi guru sekolah rendah Gwynth Vincent, penerbangan antara Kota Kinabalu dan Lahad Datu banyak menjimatkan masa, terutama ketika berdepan kecemasan keluarga atau perlu mendapatkan rawatan.
Gwynth, yang bertugas di Kota Kinabalu, berkata perjalanan darat ke kampung halamannya di Lahad Datu mengambil kira-kira lapan jam, berbanding hanya 50 minit dengan penerbangan.
Beliau pernah bergantung kepada penerbangan untuk pulang ketika neneknya sakit, selain menggunakannya bagi mendapatkan rawatan pakar mata di Kota Kinabalu.
“Dalam keadaan kecemasan, masa sangat penting,” katanya.
Menurutnya, perjalanan darat bukan sahaja mengambil masa panjang, malah memenatkan dan boleh menjadi berisiko apabila melalui jalan kurang baik serta gelap pada waktu malam.
Seorang lagi penjawat awam, Michael Roman, 28, turut memilih penerbangan bagi urusan kerja antara Kota Kinabalu dan beberapa daerah di pantai timur Sabah termasuk Lahad Datu, Sandakan dan Tawau.
Katanya, perjalanan udara mengambil masa kira-kira 45 minit hingga sejam, berbanding lapan hingga 10 jam melalui jalan darat.
Michael pernah mengambil penerbangan terakhir dari Lahad Datu ke Kota Kinabalu ketika bapa saudaranya berada dalam keadaan kritikal di hospital.
Menurutnya, kos penerbangan juga tidak jauh berbeza berbanding perjalanan darat apabila mengambil kira perbelanjaan minyak, makanan dan, dalam keadaan tertentu, tempat persinggahan untuk berehat.

Beliau menyambut baik bantuan kerajaan bagi memastikan penerbangan kekal mampu diakses, tetapi berharap kerajaan persekutuan dan negeri turut mempercepat penambahbaikan jalan raya supaya penduduk mempunyai lebih banyak pilihan pengangkutan.
Di Sarawak, penjawat awam Nuruddin Sabali, 32, menggunakan AirBorneo bagi urusan kerja, termasuk untuk perjalanan Kuching-Mukah serta Miri-Limbang dan Lawas.
Katanya, subsidi RAS wajar dikekalkan kerana penerbangan pedalaman bukan sahaja memudahkan pergerakan penduduk ke bandar utama, malah penting untuk membawa bekalan dan mendapatkan rawatan kesihatan.
“Menghapuskan subsidi akan meningkatkan kos untuk penduduk luar bandar,” katanya.
Nuruddin berkata keadaan infrastruktur di Sabah dan Sarawak juga berbeza berbanding Semenanjung, menyebabkan penerbangan kekal penting bagi sesetengah komuniti.
Akses, bukan keuntungan semata-mata

Firdausi berkata nilai penerbangan pedalaman tidak boleh diukur berdasarkan keuntungan semata-mata kerana perkhidmatan itu menyediakan akses penting kepada masyarakat yang sukar dihubungkan melalui jalan darat.

Selain memudahkan penduduk mendapatkan rawatan, katanya, penerbangan pedalaman turut membantu membawa bekalan ubat-ubatan dan membolehkan pelajar dari kawasan terpencil meneruskan pengajian di bandar.
Beliau berkata keperluan terhadap subsidi boleh berkurang sekiranya rangkaian jalan raya dan pilihan pengangkutan darat bertambah baik.
Namun, selagi penduduk masih berdepan kekangan akses, katanya, kerajaan mempunyai peranan untuk memastikan perkhidmatan penting itu terus tersedia.
“Dalam keadaan penduduk berdepan kekangan akses, kerajaan berperanan membantu melalui subsidi.
“Ini bukan soal sama ada pelaburan itu produktif atau tidak, tetapi demi kesejahteraan rakyat,” katanya.
d9b7eddb2b3fd54c: KUALA LUMPUR: Some contributed RM100, others RM300. Director Wan Nur Azwin Wan Nazrul Aisham put in RM1,000 of her own money, while another member of the team chipped in as much as RM1,200.

For a group of university students trying to make a short film, those were significant sums. But pooling their pocket money helped bring “Kola Loompor” to life - and the gamble has now paid off handsomely.
The 18-minute production by Universiti Teknologi Mara (UiTM) students picked up seven awards at the 14th Malaysian Student Film and Video Festival, including the top "Best of the Best" honour.

It also won Best Screenplay, Best Promising Director, Best Promising Actress, Best Cinematography, Best Editing and Best Production Design, while the team received a RM50,000 short-film production grant for its next project.

For Wan Nur Azwin, 24, better known as Aween Aisham, the scale of the success came as a surprise. The film had entered the festival with nine nominations, but she said the team's main hope had simply been to make their university proud.

The filmmaking itself was considerably less glamorous. Working with a limited budget, the UiTM Puncak Perdana students had no professional actors and shot the entire production outdoors around Kuala Lumpur.
Persistent rain forced them to rethink and rearrange scenes as filming progressed. But those limitations also helped give “Kola Loompor” much of its character.
The team cast a Bangladeshi supermarket worker in the leading role, reflecting a story inspired by the realities faced by migrant workers living in the capital.

The film follows Naeem, a Bangladeshi migrant worker who forms an unlikely friendship with Zainab, a local homeless woman. Their relationship eventually takes a painful turn when she disappears with his money.
Rather than presenting Kuala Lumpur through its familiar landmarks and polished cityscape, the story turns its attention towards people whose lives can easily go unnoticed within it.
For Aween, the RM50,000 production grant now offers the team something they did not have while making “Kola Loompor” - room to think beyond what they could personally afford.
She described the money spent on the film as substantial for students and said the grant had given the group fresh motivation to make their next project even stronger.

Finas chief executive officer Azmir Saifuddin Mutalib, meanwhile, said student filmmakers should use short films to build portfolios and gain exposure at festivals before moving into commercial filmmaking.
Universities, he added, are producing promising final-year projects that could potentially travel further with greater industry collaboration and support.
For the young team behind “Kola Loompor”, though, the immediate lesson may be a simpler one: a film does not necessarily need a large budget or established stars to make an impression.
Sometimes it begins with a handful of students, unpredictable weather, and whatever they can afford to pull from their own pockets.
1de577b3936a4f19: MIAMI: The United States thrashed Haiti 6-0 to surge towards the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals on Saturday as Mauricio Pochettino's penultimate game in charge ended in an emphatic victory.

Goals from Christian Pulisic (2), Auston Trusty, Julian Hall, Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun gave the US a commanding first leg advantage to all but settle the outcome of the quarter-final before Tuesday’s second leg in Cincinnati.
The build-up to Saturday's fixture in Miami had been overshadowed by news of Pochettino's departure as US coach after agreeing to take over Manchester United.

But there was little sign that news of Pochettino's exit had disturbed US preparations as they demolished World Cup qualifiers Haiti to deliver the biggest victory of the Argentine coach's two-year reign.
Trusty gave the Americans the lead after just 10 minutes, confidently finishing from close range after Sebastian Berhalter's free-kick from the right flank.
That goal was all that separated the teams at half-time but the floodgates opened after the break.
Hall calmly tucked away Antonee Robinson's low cross in the 52nd minute after a sweeping counter-attack to make it 2-0.
Pulisic made it 3-0 from the penalty spot 10 minutes later after being brought down in the box by Haiti defender Carlens Arcus.
The AC Milan forward then grabbed his second goal a minute later, rifling into the bottom corner from the edge of the area to make it 4-0.
McKennie's 68th-minute header put Pochettino's side 5-0 up and the US thought they had added a sixth soon afterwards when Balogun shrugged off Arcus to score from close range.
A VAR review, however, determined that Balogun had fouled Arcus in the build-up and the goal was chalked off.
Balogun did not have long to wait though for his 13th international goal, latching on to a Malik Tillman through ball to score in the 82nd minute.

52c53cf2eb98df59: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 15 — Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN) captured 24 of Melaka’s 28 seats in yesterday’s state election, marking the third state poll in four months where Pakatan Harapan (PH) has lost ground after Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
Here are three takeaways from the result.
BN-PAS formula delivers again
Melaka is the second consecutive state election, following Negeri Sembilan, in which BN and PN jointly outperformed PH.
Their combined tally of 24 seats edges out the 23 they won separately in 2021.

Before polling day, analysts noted that the arrangement could consolidate Malay votes, ending the vote-splitting among Umno, PAS, and Bersatu since 2018 that previously allowed PH to win multi-cornered fights.
This outcome strengthens the case for a formal BN-PN partnership heading into the 16th general election (GE16).
Still, caveats remain: parliamentary seats are larger and more diverse than state constituencies, while BN and PAS must still navigate overlapping ambitions and competing leadership interests.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Pakatan Harapan (PH) candidate for the Bukit Katil state seat Adly Zahari and PKR communications director Adam Adli hold a press conference at the PH main operations room in Melaka on November 14, 2026. — Bernama pic
Growing pressure for early GE16
Last night’s result gives BN more momentum to press for an early GE16. The call was already being made before polling day.

Umno president Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who is also deputy prime minister, said in Melaka on November 10 that it would be better to return the mandate to the people than to carry out a Cabinet reshuffle after DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke resigned as transport minister.

Analysts previously said BN and PAS are keen to capitalise on the momentum from the Negeri Sembilan, Johor and Melaka elections by pushing for an early general election. One analyst said earlier that Umno has every incentive to force an early GE16 because it thinks it is unbeatable with PAS’s support.

PH has pushed back. DAP chairman Gobind Singh Deo said BN leaders who have lost confidence in Anwar should resign from the Cabinet rather than push for dissolution, while Loke said Anwar still has a mandate and sufficient support in Parliament to continue governing.
Anwar has said the timing of GE16 depends on several factors and that any dissolution would be decided after consulting coalition partners and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) vice-president and Melaka state leadership body chairman Datuk Mohd Radzi Md Jidin (fifth from left) with the party’s eight candidates at the Bersatu candidate announcement ceremony for the 16th Melaka State Election at Baitul Tariq, Klebang, October 29, 2026. — Bernama pic
Third forces are shut out

Contesting seven seats under its own logo after falling out with PAS, Bersatu won none. The wipeout carries clear ramifications going into GE16, with PH exploring a partnership with Bersatu to counter the BN-PN cooperation.
Parti Bersama Malaysia fared no better, failing to win any of the 16 seats it contested.

Before the Melaka poll, analysts said Bersatu faced the toughest strategic crossroads, weighing reconciliation with PAS, negotiations with PH, or leading a smaller bloc of parties excluded from the BN-PN arrangement.
Every seat that went against BN fell either to PH’s urban bastions or PAS-linked PN candidates, shutting out newcomers and minor contenders.

a780f508dc3762d1: PARIS, Nov 15 — Lethal autonomous weapons powered by artificial intelligence are set to revolutionise warfare but there is no proper regulatory or legal framework governing the new technology.
A conference starting Monday at the United Nations in Geneva will discuss how to establish curbs and prohibitions on such weapons, called killer robots by some.
But some analysts doubt the discussions at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) will keep pace with the fast-changing weapons.
AFP looks at three key questions ahead of the conference.
What are LAWS?

Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) “can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks,” said Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy.

Autonomous weapons have long existed. An anti-personnel mine “is an autonomous weapon in the sense that it explodes when someone steps on it,” said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the Centre for Geopolitics of Technology at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI).

But with the proliferation of AI-enhanced drones, such weapons are now “capable of selecting and engaging a target that was not predetermined, adapting to their environment without human intervention,” said Rickli.
So the critical issue for potential regulators lies in determining the level of human control over the decision to employ such a weapon.
The United States refers to an “appropriate levels of human judgement” in the use of autonomous weapons.
France maintains that a human must remain in the decision-making loop and bans “lethal autonomous weapons systems” (LAWS) but permits “partially autonomous” systems known as PLAWS.

“The human role is always ensured through what is termed ‘appropriate control’ by a military commander – a concept that varies in scope depending on the system’s criticality and the operational context,” said Rear Admiral Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French defence ministry’s Agency for Defence Artificial Intelligence (AMIAD).
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Bavaria’s State Premier Markus Soeder (second left) and German Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche (third left) receive a briefing in front of a KNDS Dingo drone-defence vehicle equipped with Tytan drones during the opening of TYTAN Technologies’ new production facility for autonomous interceptor drones in Munich on November 9, 2026. — AFP pic
The ethical issues?

“We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, and International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric warned in a joint statement in August.
But analysts said the Geneva discussions, while important, will touch only part of the issue.
Today, the diminishing role of humans is being driven by the growing use of AI in analysis and targeting.
Rickli said the scope of the agenda in Geneva is “very narrow”.
“It fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield” – an area where its use is expanding, particularly in target generation.
He said this was seen in the US-Israeli war against Iran this year “where the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day” inside Iran.

“There are a host of problems and unacceptable risks associated with targeting and decision-support systems,” added de Roucy-Rochegonde. “Part of this debate concerns systems that are already widely deployed on the battlefield.”

“What kind of human supervision is required to ensure that the operator is genuinely exercising their own judgement rather than simply providing a rubber stamp for the machine’s recommendations?” she asked.
How quickly is the situation changing?

The autonomous weapons to be discussed in Geneva are not yet in widespread use, although analysts have noted that they have been deployed by Russia in its invasion of Ukraine as well as US attacks in Iran.
But the spread is inevitable.
“Autonomy will very quickly become a reality on the battlefield,” warned rear admiral Sebastien.
“Autonomous weapon systems are not part of a distant future – a race towards greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway,” Guterres and Spoljaric said in their statement.

Yet significant doubts and dangers remain, Dario Amodei, head of the AI giant Anthropic, warned this year: “Today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”
But ultimately, the incentive for major powers is too strong.
Swarms of autonomous drones – which “aim to neutralise an adversary through saturation” – would be highly effective, and some states view them as a crucial strategic advantage, said Rickli.
In January, the Chinese defence ministry described swarms of autonomous drones as the “new face of warfare.”

“In an era of sharp military competition, the first state to normalise fully autonomous lethal strikes will reset expectations for everyone else,” said Gerald Mako, a research affiliate of Cambridge University in the Small Wars Journal. — AFP
43f9e2a79705a30c: YANGON, Nov 15 — Myanmar faces a pivotal week as neighbouring nations weigh the future of post-coup relations, while the United Nations’ top court threatens a verdict of genocide over its dark past.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is scheduled on Thursday to rule whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.
The case looms over a three-day meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) due to debate its policy freezing Myanmar out of summits since a 2021 putsch.
Rohingya activists say the pending judgement should haunt the minds of Asean leaders when they meet in the Philippines starting Sunday.

“We are waiting to see what the outcome will be on that day, the judgement for everything we have been experiencing for generations,” said a 25-year-old Yangon-based Rohingya activist who requested anonymity for security reasons.
“If they welcome people who lack basic humanity and destroyed our lives, our futures and our possessions, we will be very let down,” he added.
Man in question
The UN court case and Asean’s diplomatic dilemma are separate issues on paper. But both converge on one man: Min Aung Hlaing.
The 11-nation Asean bloc has shunned Myanmar leaders from summits since his military coup turfed out the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and sparked civil war.
The Hague case dates back to 2017, when Myanmar is accused of breaching the United Nations Genocide Convention by brutalising the Rohingya.
The judgement due Thursday will weigh state culpability, not individual guilt.
But Min Aung Hlaing led the military as it spearheaded the mass killings, rape and arson targeting the Rohingya and driving nearly 750,000 into Bangladesh as refugees.
This April, he was installed as president after elections rejected by democracy watchdogs, and is waging a charm offensive seeking acceptance in the diplomatic fold.
“If the ICJ finds that Myanmar committed genocide, it would seriously weaken Min Aung Hlaing’s efforts,” said Wai Yan Phyo Naing, visiting scholar at Taiwan’s Academia Sinica.
“Any public association with him could create political and reputational risks, especially for governments that claim to support human rights and international law.”
Signs of support
But Myanmar has already secured signals of support to return to Asean.
As civilian president, Min Aung Hlaing has had red-carpet welcomes in bloc members Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam.
Even Muslim-majority Malaysia hosted him last month, albeit to expedite the return of thousands of Myanmar migrants as a wave of prejudice towards Rohingya refugees swept the nation.

Rights groups expressed alarm about the fate of those returned, but that did not prevent Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim promising “Malaysia will do whatever is possible” to smooth Myanmar’s normalisation in Asean.
Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group, said the ICJ ruling may have little impact on Min Aung Hlaing’s momentum.
“Governments willing to host him are unlikely to change course over a ruling addressed to the Myanmar state, which places no legal restriction on him personally,” he said.
“It may make some members more cautious about being seen to move quickly, but I doubt it will stop the drift towards normalisation.”
Diplomatic drift
Some analysts argue that a finding Myanmar committed genocide may actually embolden Min Aung Hlaing, confirming he can rub shoulders with world leaders regardless.
It may also stoke division between Asean nations arguing he should be ostracised and those favouring engagement to coax Myanmar towards a different future.
Post-coup Myanmar has been represented by senior civil servants at Asean summits, an arrangement which will remain in place for the Manila meeting.
The bloc’s rotating chair will at the end of this year pass from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalising Myanmar ties.
But in 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.
Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said Thursday he did not forsee the ICJ ruling would disrupt the process of “calibrated re-engagement”.
“Asean is unlikely to fully embrace Min Aung Hlaing at a summit level soon,” said independent Myanmar analyst David Mathieson.
“But it’s only a matter of time.” — AFP

7a98f561f849cd66: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo taken by Rahul Ingle, May 2012. This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain. These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging. In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
A school without walls

In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees. The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat. Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique. At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity. In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years. This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Language, culture, and the role of the state<!--TgQPHd|||[[2,[null,null,1,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,[351768,null,0]],[],null,1]]-->

Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension. In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service. Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling. However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history. Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion. Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology. In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Risks and potential

Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system. While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers. This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Talking about artificial intelligence in outdoor classrooms may seem contradictory at first glance, but it is precisely in these contexts that technology needs to be considered creatively and responsibly, not as a replacement for the essential, but as a strategic complement.

The priority remains clear: Building schools, training teachers, and ensuring access to basic materials. The question is how to integrate developed technology without creating profound inequalities, respecting local contexts, and placing the student and teacher at the center of decision-making. In a country where learning still takes place under trees, the future of education will depend not only on the technology available, but also on the political and social choices that define who has access to knowledge and under what conditions.

It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day.

I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning?

They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for.

In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?”

We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions.
[Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight.

They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology.

The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.”
Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with.

It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined.
There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate?

A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey.

I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do.

There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events.

You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well.

This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means.

It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well.

Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?”

The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app.

I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that.

That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do.

That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding.

For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.”

It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster.

A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up.

At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people.

How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference.
Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now. Have a good time.” And he ended the call.
Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed?

I actually wrote something about this. I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI.

There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.”

That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things.

088d1c55b762379a: <!--kg-card-begin: html-->
<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Humans watching monkeys watching Minions
Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.

“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.

Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick, The Peanut Butter Falcon, Whiplash, Room, Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, The Tomorrow Man, Dom Hemingway, Life After Beth, Woodshock, and The Comedian.
“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said.

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present, and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques.

Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.

“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.

In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.
In other news…
Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice
Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE.

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.
Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?
Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh
Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One.

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.
The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning
Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study.

“We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
037e089a5d550c90: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

77103068193881cc: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.
As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.
A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."
A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.
Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.
"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

651774b405c45576: BERLIN: Solar energy’s contribution to Germany’s net electricity generation is fast approaching a record of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year, reported the German Press Agency (dpa).

By Sept 27, solar output had already reached 90.2 terawatt-hours, surpassing the 90 terawatt-hours generated during the whole of 2025, according to the German Solar Association (BSW-Solar), based in Berlin.

An unusually high number of sunshine hours and the continued expansion of photovoltaic capacity contributed to the figures, the association said, citing a generation update released by the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE on Saturday.
By contrast, 20 years ago, solar power generated just 2.2 terawatt-hours over an entire year.
The approaching record marks a milestone in Germany’s energy transition, said Carsten Kornig, managing director of BSW-Solar.
“Photovoltaics has developed from a niche technology into a cornerstone of our electricity supply,” Kornig said.
“Society as a whole benefits from this: through cheaper electricity, fewer energy imports and significantly lower climate-related damage.”
An electricity output of 100 terawatt-hours represents an enormous amount of energy. One terawatt-hour is equivalent to one billion kilowatt-hours.
For comparison, Hamburg consumed 10.7 terawatt-hours of electricity last year.
Households in Germany typically consume between 2,000 and 4,000 kilowatt-hours a year.
According to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office, 59.1% of all electricity generated domestically in the first half of 2026 came from renewable sources
Photovoltaics accounted for 17.8% of total domestic electricity generation, making it the country’s third-largest electricity source, behind wind power, the leading source, and coal.
